title: There Is No Boomer Succession Plan
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn examines how Boomer institutional leaders have systematically failed to develop successors of comparable stature, leaving organizations structurally dependent on irreplaceable figures. Using Anna Wintour's Met Gala legacy, Mitch Daniels at Purdue, and Tim Keller at Redeemer Presbyterian as case studies, he argues that top Boomer leaders typically surrounded themselves with subordinates rather than potential successors -- people who would never challenge the boss. Institutions are now responding by building endowments to sustain operations after the Boomer era ends rather than trying to replicate the leader's singular influence. Renn suggests this 'endowment over succession' move is often the smart play given the reality that no successor could match the original. Yet he warns that optimizing around an individual at the expense of institutional longevity is ultimately harmful, and that America's national debt -- growing from $3T to $39T during the Boomer presidential era -- is the same pattern at national scale.
points: * Boomer leaders like Wintour, Daniels, and Keller invested heavily in talent-development rhetoric but failed to produce successors of comparable accomplishment. * The Met's solution -- building a $100M+ endowment from Wintour's final high-earning years -- exemplifies 'structuring around absence' rather than developing a replacement. * Top Boomer leaders tended to surround themselves with people who would never plausibly equal or upstage the boss, which may explain the succession gap. * Tim Keller raised ~$100M and split Redeemer into three smaller churches before retiring -- a recognition that no single successor could hold the enterprise in its prior form. * America's national debt grew from $3T to $39T during the Boomer presidential era, the largest-scale instance of optimizing present returns at future generations' expense.
quotes: That failure seems characteristic of very top tier Boomer leaders. From what I've observed, they saw themselves as talent developers, but were unable to successfully create successors or proteges of similar accomplishment.
When there's no obvious high stature successor, or institutional sustainability is in question, institutions where it's feasible should be thinking about this kind of approach.
Her successor will never have the ability to do what Wintour herself did with it, regardless of how talented that successor might be.

As a rule, institutions should not allow themselves to become over-optimized around a single person (or generation), no matter how talented, in ways that sacrifices the long-term trajectory of the institution or future generations.
Part of leaving a place better than when you found it means making sure its future stewards have the same or better opportunities than you had.

Perhaps the most important part of getting through the American Transition is to reset the game board here, so that people think they are on a personal, institutional, and national upward escalator extending behind and ahead of them through time.
